name: Tompkins County (Town of Dryden)

actions.title: Town of Dryden 18-Month Data Center & Crypto Mining Moratorium
actions.summary: The Dryden Town Board adopted an 18-month moratorium on data center and cryptocurrency mine development in July 2024, triggered by an out-of-state developer's application to build near State Route 13.

actions.title: Town of Dryden Permanent Zoning Ban on Data Centers and Cryptocurrency Mines
actions.summary: The Dryden Town Board unanimously amended the zoning code to define data centers and cryptocurrency mines as prohibited land uses in all zones, making Dryden the first town in New York State to ban data centers outright.

actions.title: Town of Danby Zoning Amendment Banning Data Centers
actions.summary: The Danby Town Board defined data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities in its zoning code and excluded them from all permitted uses, effectively banning both.

actions.title: Town of Enfield Proposed Data Center Ban or Restriction Ordinance
actions.summary: The Enfield Town Board was actively debating whether to impose an outright ban similar to Dryden's or to permit data centers with tight regulation, driven by community concern over the TeraWulf Cayuga Power Plant proposal in neighboring Lansing.

contextBlurb: Tompkins County became the epicenter of New York's municipal data center backlash, with the Town of Dryden making history in February 2026 as the first municipality in the state to permanently ban data centers via a zoning update after an 18-month moratorium. The controversy was catalyzed by TeraWulf's proposal to convert the former Cayuga Power Plant in the neighboring Town of Lansing into a large AI data center, which sparked packed town meetings and a 16,000-signature petition. Multiple surrounding towns—Danby, Enfield, Ulysses, and Newfield—subsequently moved to adopt their own restrictions.

name: Genesee County

actions.title: GCEDC SEQR Retraction for Stream Data Centers STAMP Project (First Proposal)
actions.summary: The Genesee County Economic Development Center (GCEDC) board voted unanimously to retract the State Environmental Quality Review for Stream Data Centers' initial STAMP project after the Tonawanda Seneca Nation and Sierra Club filed suit alleging inadequate environmental review.

actions.title: DEC Declines Lead Agency Status; Directs GCEDC to Conduct Deeper Environmental Review
actions.summary: The New York DEC declined to take over as lead agency for the STAMP data center environmental review but directed the GCEDC to conduct a significantly more thorough review, citing unanswered questions about noise, proximity to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation, and the project's limited job creation relative to its scale.

actions.title: GCEDC Approves Financial Assistance Review for Stream Data Centers' $19.5B Revised STAMP Proposal
actions.summary: Despite widespread community opposition, the GCEDC board unanimously voted to begin reviewing a financial assistance application from Stream Data Centers for a revised $19.5 billion, 2.2 million-square-foot hyperscale data center campus at STAMP, including a proposed $1.46 billion in tax abatements.

contextBlurb: Genesee County is home to the most contested data center proposal in New York: Stream Data Centers' 'Project Double Reed' at the STAMP industrial park in the Town of Alabama, which grew from a $6.3 billion to a $19.5 billion campus backed by Apollo Global Management. The Tonawanda Seneca Nation, whose reservation territory directly borders the STAMP site, has led legal and regulatory challenges citing noise, air pollution, and failure to conduct meaningful tribal consultation. Residents strongly oppose over $1.46 billion in proposed tax subsidies, while county officials view data center revenue as essential to funding a $150 million water infrastructure upgrade.

name: Onondaga County (Town of Lysander)

actions.title: Town of Lysander Six-Month Data Center Construction Moratorium
actions.summary: The Lysander Town Board unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on data center development, spurred by over 350 residents attending a public meeting to oppose the proposed 300 MW Ranalli Lysander Data Center on a 120-acre industrial-zoned site.

actions.title: Onondaga County $500K Data Center Impact Study
actions.summary: Onondaga County launched a $500,000 consultant-led study to assess the land use, zoning, water, wastewater, noise, and environmental impacts of data centers, providing guidance to towns including Lysander, Dewitt, Salina, and Manlius that have paused data center development.

contextBlurb: The Town of Lysander in Onondaga County became a focal point of upstate New York's data center debate after Ranalli Super DC, LLC applied to connect a proposed 300 MW facility to the NYISO grid in May 2025. Community group 'Citizens Against Lysander Data Center' organized intense opposition, leading to a unanimous town board moratorium in May 2026 attended by more than 350 residents. Onondaga County responded county-wide by commissioning a $500,000 study and noting that multiple towns—Lysander, Dewitt, Salina, and Manlius—had already paused development.

name: Fulton County (Town of Perth)

actions.title: Town of Perth One-Year Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: The Perth Town Board passed a one-year moratorium on the development of any data centers, with Town Supervisor Greg Fagan citing concerns over energy usage and the desire to maintain local control over land-use decisions.

contextBlurb: The Town of Perth in Fulton County was among the earliest New York municipalities to act, passing a one-year preemptive data center moratorium in June 2025 before any specific proposal materialized. Supervisor Greg Fagan framed it as a protective measure against energy demand spikes, building on the town's prior experience with moratoriums on solar, wind, and battery storage facilities. The action preceded the state legislature's broader moratorium effort by nearly a year.

name: St. Lawrence County

actions.title: St. Lawrence County Resolution Affirming Local Authority Over Data Center Siting
actions.summary: Rather than passing a full moratorium, St. Lawrence County passed a resolution asserting local governmental authority over data center siting decisions and urging all municipalities within the county to exercise that authority carefully.

contextBlurb: St. Lawrence County chose a measured approach in June 2026, stopping short of a full moratorium but passing a formal resolution affirming that local governments—not state agencies or developers—hold primary authority over where data centers are sited. The move reflected growing concern among rural upstate counties about losing local control to large-scale infrastructure projects driven by AI demand. The resolution urged all municipalities in the county to take an active role in any review process.
